A GIC ladder can keep its principal while its interest income falls after renewal

Four charts follow a hypothetical renewing five-rung ladder, separating interest receipts, rolled principal and the outside reserve needed when new rates differ.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Trace interest income while each rung renews at a different assumed rate

Interactive planning lab

Annual interest in the first modeled year$2,000
Annual interest after all first renewals$1,000
Outside opening reserve required across ten years$7,000

Hypothetical five-rung ladder with equal principal, initial maturities at the ends of years 1–5, and annual cash interest paid before that year’s spending. Every initial rung uses the same entered rate regardless of term. Each maturing principal is immediately reinvested for five years at the entered renewal rate, including subsequent renewals; neither quoted rates nor future availability are predicted. The old rate pays through its maturity year and the renewed rate begins the following year. All principal stays invested and nominal principal remains unchanged. Interest is paid outside the ladder rather than compounded. Outside cash earns zero; annual spending is fixed. No tax, inflation, default, deposit-insurance assessment, fees, early redemption or within-year cash timing is modeled. Negative outside cash is an unmet funding need, not a sale of principal or an automatic loan.

On this page

  1. Distinguish a guaranteed term from an unknown renewal rate
  2. Write the five-rung schedule before counting the receipts
  3. Keep the old rate through the final year of its original term
  4. Do not spend the same matured principal that the model renews

The central idea

A maturity date gives a choice about principal. If that principal is reinvested, the same dollars are unavailable for spending, and the new interest income still depends on the renewal rate.

01

Distinguish a guaranteed term from an unknown renewal rate

A fixed rate for one deposit term does not specify the rate available when that term ends. A plan that intends to reinvest principal needs a separate assumption for the next contract.

The Ontario Securities Commission’s investor-education guide describes reinvestment risk as the possibility of reinvesting principal or income at a lower rate. This article isolates principal renewal while interest is paid out for spending. It makes no prediction about future market rates.

A ladder spreads initial maturity dates across several years. That changes when different parts of principal encounter the renewal assumption. It does not lock every later term at today’s selected rate or turn an entered future rate into a guarantee.

02

Write the five-rung schedule before counting the receipts

The example divides CAD 50,000 equally into five CAD 10,000 rungs. Their initial terms mature at the ends of years one, two, three, four and five. All five initially pay 4% in annual cash interest, even though the terms differ. That equal-rate starting point is a teaching assumption, not a set of available quotes.

At each maturity, the whole CAD 10,000 principal is immediately renewed for five years at the selected 2%. One rung therefore matures each year, including years six through ten. Later renewals use the same 2% assumption, with no new rate scenario introduced.

OSC’s GIC explanation describes staggered maturities and choices at maturity, including reinvestment or taking cash. Here renewal is an explicit instruction in the model. The charts do not infer an actual bank’s automatic-renewal terms.

03

Keep the old rate through the final year of its original term

Year one receives five interest payments of CAD 400, for CAD 2,000 in total. The first rung matures only after paying that year’s interest. Its renewed rate therefore begins contributing to the cash schedule in year two.

Year two has four original payments of CAD 400 and one renewed payment of CAD 200, totaling CAD 1,800. Year three has three original and two renewed payments, totaling CAD 1,600. The later totals are CAD 1,400 in year four and CAD 1,200 in year five.

In year six all five rungs pay CAD 200, so annual interest is CAD 1,000. With every later renewal held at 2%, income stays at that level through year ten. The composition chart explains the transition rather than implying that all the original 4% income disappears at the first maturity.

04

Do not spend the same matured principal that the model renews

Each year CAD 10,000 comes due and is immediately committed to another five-year term. It is a return and reinvestment of principal, not new interest earned. Counting it as spending money while also retaining the renewed rung would create resources twice.

Across ten years the schedule rolls CAD 100,000 of gross maturity principal. That does not mean the household began with CAD 100,000 or earned that much. The original CAD 50,000 is being reused as different rungs reach maturity again.

Nominal principal remains CAD 50,000 throughout this illustration, while total interest paid outside it is CAD 13,000. That interest is a distinct stream. The tool does not compound it back into the ladder, assume access to locked principal, or replace a spending shortfall with a redemption.

05

Put the interest income beside the spending assigned to it

The selected annual cash need is CAD 2,000, received interest arrives before that year’s spending, and the outside reserve starts at CAD 1,000. Year one uses its CAD 2,000 interest without drawing the reserve. Later income falls while the assigned need stays fixed.

The first gaps are CAD 200, CAD 400 and CAD 600 in years two, three and four. Outside cash is therefore CAD 800, CAD 400 and negative CAD 200 after those years. An unchanged principal does not remove that spending shortage.

By the end of year ten, cumulative gaps total CAD 7,000: CAD 20,000 of assigned spending less CAD 13,000 of interest. The required outside opening reserve is CAD 7,000, while the entered CAD 1,000 leaves CAD 6,000 still to fund. The matrix varies renewal rates and annual needs to show how that requirement changes.

Holding the initial 4% and CAD 2,000 annual need unchanged, a 1% renewal assumption requires CAD 10,500 outside the ladder. A 3% assumption requires CAD 3,500. Both cases preserve the same CAD 50,000 of nominal principal. The difference comes from thirty-five renewed rung-years across the ten-year window: one extra percentage point on each CAD 10,000 rung supplies CAD 3,500 more interest in total. That is a sensitivity of the selected calendar, rather than a claim that a higher rate will be available.

These annual points also simplify payment timing. An interest deposit at year-end cannot pay a bill due months earlier. A real implementation needs exact interest dates, a within-year cash calendar and a separate review of whether preserving every rung’s principal remains appropriate.

06

Review the actual maturity instructions and the wider plan

FCAC’s GIC rights guide identifies information about the term, principal repayment, interest payments and renewal conditions that applicable federally regulated institutions must disclose. Read the new rate and instructions before treating a maturity as a continuation of the same income.

The tool excludes tax, inflation, fees, issuer failure, insurance eligibility and any market value before maturity. The nominal principal line is therefore not proof of maintained purchasing power, complete protection or personal suitability. The interest figures are before tax, and annual spending does not rise with prices.

Record the intended job of each maturity: renewal, spending or another goal. Then use the corresponding cash treatment consistently. Stress the rate that would fund the next term, and keep reserves already assigned to other bills separate. A ladder is a schedule to manage, rather than a promise that its first year’s income continues indefinitely.
